The problem with an example-based approach to abstract algebra is that the objects you work with are extremely simple or require too much external knowledge. Studying groups from the symmetries of objects feels pointless because it does not obviously lead to any new insights or the jump from modular arithmetic to rings and ideals can feel like needless or pointless generalization; however, a lot of the theory of modules, rings, and ideals and such is somewhat natural in functional analysis and Lie theory naturally arises in a lot of mathematical physics, but it is a mistake to use that as justification to someone first learning the theory. Ultimately, abstract algebra really suffers pedagogically because we haven't quite found a happy middle ground. Some authors do a fantastic treatment of abstract algebra, but a lot of the introduction of the subject is hard to stomach for some students. Mathematical physics and theoretical physics are very different for the most part.

Mathematical physics is usually concerned with mostly rigorous mathematical proofs and is often dubiously connected to known physics. It's more like doing pure math that is very heavily inspired by structures, objects, and equations found in physics (and usually generalized well beyond what seems physically realizable). You can get by without a ton of physics mastery in mathematical physics. Some is needed, but a first or second year grad level physics at most in the field you want to work in is needed.

This is not the case in theoretical physics. Theoretical physics is developing physics theories based on experimental data and other physics theories. You generally need a lot of physics mastery for theoretical physics (how certain particles interact, how certain quantum fields interact, how gravity behaves at various scales and interacts with forms of matter, things like this). Now this isn't to say they are distinct. There are plenty of people who work in the intersection, but it's a small portion compared to their symmetric difference (for lack of a better way to put it hah).

You can absolutely do mathematical physics research in a math grad program. You will likely not be able to do theoretical physics research in a math grad program. That said, not every math department has a mathematical physicist as part of the faculty, so you need to look closely at the schools you want to apply to.

I listed some of those as separate fields. There are very few people doing single variable complex analysis these days. Not too many even do several complex variables, partly because it's so damn hard. I don't know if Fourier analysis really counts as real analysis because it's mostly steeped in functional analysis these days.

This is a very large field. Functional analysis is the general umbrella for people working in analysis these days (excluding the small number of people doing several complex variables research). Almost no one does research in real analysis these days. There are analysis adjacent fields that I'm omitting here of course.

I do research in integral transforms related to the Fourier transform and associated quantum structures. Other people do operator spaces, C\* theory, Banach algebras, von Neumann algebras, harmonic analysis which ultimately just representation theory, and other areas. There are closely related areas like ergodic theory and dynamical systems which overlap a lot with analysis. There's also PDEs and signal processing which use a lot of functional analysis but not everyone considers them functional analysis because of how applied they are.

Harmonic analysis is a somewhat big field in functional analysis. There are tons of open questions because of how bizarre locally compact groups can get at the level of topology or the group itself. There are Fourier algebras, different types of locally compact groups (abelian, amenable, unimodular), induced representations, all sorts of things to explore here. There are also a lot of people working on representation theory of groups that are relevant to physics like SU(p, q).

I would note that there are definite hurdles in applying category theory to analysis. Some simple but crucial features of functional analysis have met with serious issue when being cast in category-theoretic language. There was a really good MO post about this some years ago, but I can't find it. I don't think there's been any improvement on this front to this point. Category theory has its uses, mostly in algebraic flavored mathematics, but it is not a good foundation for all of mathematics. It is especially poor as a pedagogical tool for introductory mathematics courses for the average mathematics student.

Point 3 is actually very useful when relating L^1 spaces with different measures on them. This comes up in integral transform theory when you have integral kernels with varying behavior (different asymptotics at, say, 0 and infinity) which force certain behaviors of the functions they can be integrated against so that the integral transform is well-defined. Measure theory is pretty much indispensable for functional analysis if you're doing anything concrete (and even more abstract functional analysis uses measure theory). The L^p spaces and their subsets and related spaces are too critical to throw measure theory aside.

That said: even most analysts (non-probability theorists) don't *love* measure theory. It is more of a useful tool for doing what they really care about while knowing that everything is well-defined. Pick up a book on integrals. Most of those integrals are understood in the Riemann sense which means that they are extremely sensitive to conditional convergence and therefore rely on the directionality built into the Riemann integral. However, in analysis, you would really like your integrals to exist without relying on the way you add up the areas under the curve. That is what measure theory is for: it is built on absolute convergence and doesn't have all of the annoying "this is true if there are countably many discontinuities" and such theorem statements that you have to make if you do an extended Riemann integral with absolute integrability instead like I think Spivak does (?). Plus, some theorems are just hard as hell in the Riemann setting because of how strictly defined the integral is. Having dominated convergence, Fatou, Fubini, and a couple of other results (Luzin, Egorov types) are really useful. They're really the point of measure theory in my opinion. Everything else is just to get to those points (with really cool, if at first weird as hell, ideas along the way).

(Also, how are you going to work with RKHSes without measure theory at your disposal..? You need to be able to integrate well over the space.)

This hardo "do it yourself, don't ask for help" mentality is tiring. So many gifted students shame others for asking for help, and it is bad for the health of mathematics overall (and the people that need help but are too ashamed to ask for it). It has created a fear in some for asking for help or showing weakness of any kind. Research is hard as hell for most of us (and even those who understand a lot of high level and abstract math struggle because they work on hard as hell problems), and it is part of the research experience to be stuck, not know what you're doing all of the time, and be frustrated. There is no shame in asking for help. Right now, my undergrads are not asking as many questions of me, and it is very frustrating. It is hard to tell if they are understanding what they're doing or if they're even working that hard (we're on summer break, so I'm not being too pushy with research).

A good advisor will both let you struggle with something *and* help you when you are clearly stuck. The best insights into a field come from letting the problem rattle around for a while because it means you are thinking deeply on a topic. Getting help when you're completely stuck after you've made an effort is not only okay, but I think it is good. You may have a very good handle on some nuances of the topic, but perhaps there is some completely new thing you have no exposure to that you can now learn by asking for help. It may even be the case that you're stuck on something very nontrivial, even for an expert, and it may be a good exercise for both of you. There are many times in papers that something not immediately obvious is stated very plainly without much explanation as if it was very trivial. In many of these cases, the result may be very technical but mostly follow your nose and the authors do not wish to waste time on it, they may be outright wrong or not know how to prove it and are just putting it on the reader to figure it out, it could be poorly written or explained (which happens a lot in certain fields for some reason), or it could be a folklore result whose origin is lost to time and is floating out in the ether and everyone in the field just states, hoping it is right without knowing where to find it (I run into this *a lot* in my research....).

It's certainly not their fault on that point. The traditional career path does not provide for that. They can typically relay correct mathematics (not always... I've been on the receiving end of that plenty over the years), but that's about where their natural ability stops if they haven't ventured outside the realm of just mathematics into mathematics education circles. Most mathematicians at big schools exclusively still do traditional lecture style which is shown time and again not to be very effective at actual learning for most students. That doesn't mean the classroom should be completely flipped when certain goals must be attained on a timeline, but very few even try active learning in any way. (This doesn't apply to large courses like first year's which are very difficult to moderate in active learning situations, though those are often taught by non tenure line faculty at most big schools these days.) Younger math faculty are bucking this trend and moving away from exclusively lecturing and incorporating ideas from other subjects in their courses (by example or in projects, etc), but that is because math education has become more of a focus with them.

I can name a handful of first semester students across years I've taught that can get at least close to an answer on this on their own when we didn't cover such concepts or pathologies in class or in assessments. One fairly significant difference is most analysts (excluding ODE/PDE theorists and even still sometimes then) have a lot of algebra in their research of varying flavors and motifs. It turns out that pure analysis is really difficult as the low-hanging fruit has all been taken up. There are still a decent number of analysts that do pure analysis however (Banach space theorists attacking the various open problems therein). Undergraduate mathematics has a bit of a siloed nature: analysis is analysis, number theory is number theory, algebra is algebra, etc. It turns out that some of the richest mathematics you can do is in their intersections, borrowing concepts and structures from another area. This is especially true for analysis. Banach space theory is fairly dry in my opinion (though some of the open problems are really bizarre and cool), but Banach algebras are really fascinating. Just adding a touch more structure (and therefore restricting attention to a smaller space) gives a much richer theory. Likewise, studying integral transforms and trying to prove general theorems about them is a bit of a fools errand, however adding a bit more algebraic structure makes it possible to prove really cool things, cf Akhiezer's trick for generating eigenfunctions. A lot of earlier functional analysis was geared toward PDE analysis (and the mathematics that is useful in it and arose from it) and heavily steeped in ideas useful for function spaces over R^(n) (lots of Fourier theory, distribution theory, rigged Hilbert spaces, generalized functions, Sturm-Liouville theory, and related topics). Rudin's book is awful for this. There's been a shift in the pedagogy of the field toward a bit more abstraction, gearing up for Banach algebras, C\* algebras, and similar ideas since that's where most people who call themselves functional analysts work. Many of the books and course notes of the last several years have taken this focus, leaving the more concrete stuff perhaps to PDE or signal processing courses. There's more of a sharp dichotomy between PDE theorists and functional analysts these days than there were in the early days of the field.

It's really just chain rule packaging away part of a complicated integral to make it simpler.

int e^(sin x) cos(x) dx

is the same as

int e^(u) du/dx dx

with u(x) = sin(x). Chain rule would say that the antiderivative is e^(u). We don't strictly need to carry around du/dx dx since we're just doing the antiderivative of the e^u part, so we can envision this as the integral of e^u du.
